chunks: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Musa ibn Babawayh al-Qummi (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Musa (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Kufi al-Asadi narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Barmaki narrated to us. He said: Abdullah ibn Ahmad narrated to us. He said: Isma'il ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, from Thabit ibn Dinar al-Thumali, from the Master of Worshippers Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon them), who said:
The right of your self upon you is that you employ it in the obedience of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

And the right of the tongue is that you consider it too noble for obscenity, accustom it to good, refrain from any meddling in which there is nothing to be gained, express kindness to the people, and speak well concerning them.

And the right of hearing is to keep it pure from listening to backbiting and listening to that to which it is unlawful to listen. And the right of sight is that you lower it before everything which is unlawful for you, and that you take heed whenever you look at anything. And the right of your hand is that you stretch it not toward that which is unlawful for you.

And the right of your two legs is that you walk not with them toward that which is unlawful for you. You will stand upon the Path with them, so see to it that they do not slip and cause you to fall into the Fire. And the right of your stomach is that you make it not into a container for the forbidden, and you eat no more than your fill. And the right of your private part is that you protect it from fornication, and guard it against being looked upon.

And the right of prayer is that you know it is an arrival before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that you are standing before Allah. When you know that, you will stand in the station of the lowly, vile, beseeching, fearful, hopeful, afraid, abased, imploring one, magnifying the One before whom you stand with stillness and dignity. You approach it with your heart and perform it within its bounds and rights.

And the right of fasting is that you know it is a veil which Allah has set up over your tongue, hearing, sight, stomach, and private part to protect you from the Fire. If you abandon the fast, you have torn Allah's protective covering from yourself.

And the right of charity is that you know it is a storing away with your Lord, and a deposit needing no witnesses. If you deposit it in secret, you are more confident than depositing it publicly. Know that it repels afflictions and illnesses in this world and repels the Fire in the Hereafter.

And the right of Hajj is that you know it is an arrival before your Lord, a flight from your sins; through it your repentance is accepted and the obligation Allah imposed upon you is fulfilled. And the right of the offering is that you desire Allah through it, not His creation; you desire exposure to Allah's mercy and salvation of your spirit on the day you meet Him.

And the right of the ruler is that you know you were made a trial for him, that he is tested through you by what Allah gave him of authority over you, and that you should not expose yourself to his displeasure, casting yourself into destruction and becoming his partner in whatever evil he brings upon you.

And the right of the one who trains you through knowledge is magnifying him, respecting his sessions, listening well and attending devotedly. Do not raise your voice toward him nor answer anyone who asks him, let him answer. Do not speak to anyone or backbite in his session. Defend him when ill-spoken of, conceal his faults, manifest his virtues. Do not sit with his enemy or oppose his friend. If you do this, Allah's angels will testify that you went to him and learned for Allah's sake, not for people.

As for the right of master through property, obey him except in disobedience to Allah, for there is no obedience to a creature in disobedience to the Creator. As for the right of subjects through authority, know they became subjects through weakness and your strength. You must act justly, be like a compassionate father, forgive their ignorance, not hasten punishment, and thank Allah for power over them.

As for the right of subjects through knowledge, know that Allah made you a caretaker through knowledge He gave you and wisdom He opened for you. If you teach well without harshness or annoyance, Allah increases His bounty. But if you withhold knowledge or are harsh when sought, Allah will strip you of knowledge and its splendour and remove your place from hearts.

As for the right of the wife, know that Allah made her your tranquility and comfort. Know this is Allah's blessing, so honour her and be gentle. Though your right over her is greater, she has the right to compassion, for she is your captive whom you feed and clothe, and when she errs in ignorance, you pardon her.

As for the right of your slave, know he is your Lord's creature, the son of your father and mother, your flesh and blood. You did not make him; Allah made him. You created none of his limbs nor provide his sustenance, but Allah sufficed that, then subjected him to you and entrusted him to you. So treat him well as Allah treated you well. If you dislike him, replace him, but do not torment Allah's creature. There is no strength save in Allah.

As for the right of your mother, know she carried you where none carries anyone, gave you of her heart's fruit what none gives, and protected you with all her limbs. She cared not if she hungered while feeding you, thirsted while giving you drink, was naked while clothing you, or suffered sun while shading you. She gave up sleep for you and protected you from heat and cold. You cannot thank her except through Allah's help. As for your father's right, know he is your root; without him you would not exist. Whatever pleases you in yourself, know your father is the root of that blessing. So praise Allah and thank Him accordingly. There is no strength save in Allah.

As for your child's right, know he is from you and attributed to you in this world's affairs with his good and evil. You are responsible for his good upbringing, guiding him to his Lord, and helping him obey. Act as one who knows he will be rewarded for good and punished for ill. As for your brother's right, know he is your hand, honour, and strength. Do not use him as a weapon for disobedience or equipment for wronging Allah's creatures. Do not abandon helping him. If he obeys Allah, good; otherwise, let Allah be more honoured. There is no strength save in Allah.

As for the right of your master who freed you, know he spent his property for you, brought you from bondage's abasement to freedom's honour, freed you from captivity, loosened slavery's bonds, gave you ownership of yourself, and freed you for worship. Know he is closest to you in life and death, and helping him is incumbent. There is no strength save in Allah. As for the right of the slave you freed, know that Allah made your freeing him a means to Him and veil against the Fire. Your immediate reward is inheriting from him if he has no family, and your ultimate reward is Paradise.

As for the right of the benefactor, thank him, mention his kindness, speak well of him, and sincerely supplicate for him before Allah. Then if able, repay him. As for the muezzin's right, know he reminds you of your Lord, calls you to your fortune, and helps you fulfil Allah's obligation. Thank him as you would a benefactor.

As for the right of your prayer imam, know he took on ambassadorship between you and your Lord. He speaks for you, not you for him; supplicates for you, not you for him. He spared you the terror of standing before Allah. If deficient, it belongs to him; if perfect, you are his partner with no superiority. He protected himself through himself and his prayer through his prayer. Thank him accordingly.

As for the sitting companion's right, treat him gently, be fair in discussion, do not leave without his permission. He who sits with you may leave without yours. Forget his slips, remember his good, let him hear only good. As for the neighbor's right, guard him absent, honour him present, help him when wronged. Do not pursue his faults; if you know evil, conceal it. If he accepts counsel, counsel privately. Do not abandon him in difficulty, forgive his sin, associate generously. There is no strength save in Allah.

As for the companion's right, accompany him with bounty and fairness. Honour him as he honours you. Do not let him outdo you in generosity. Wish for him as he wishes for you, restrain him from sin. Be mercy, not punishment. There is no strength save in Allah. As for the partner's right, if absent look after his affairs, if present show regard. Make no decision without him, do nothing without consulting. Guard his property, betray him not. Allah's hand is over two partners who do not betray each other. There is no strength save in Allah.

As for your property's right, take only from the lawful, spend only in the proper. Do not prefer over yourself those who will not praise you. Act in obedience to your Lord, do not be miserly lest you fall into regret. There is no strength save in Allah. As for the creditor's right, if you have means give him; if in hardship, satisfy with good words and send away gently. The associate's right is not to deceive, cheat, or trick him, and fear Allah in his affair.

The adversary who claims against you: if his claim is true, witness against yourself, do not wrong him, give his due. If false, be gentle, show only kindness, do not displease your Lord. There is no strength save in Allah. Your adversary against whom you claim: if right, be polite; if wrong, fear Allah, repent, and abandon the claim. The one seeking advice: if he has good opinion, advise accordingly; if not, direct him to one who knows. The advisor: do not accuse him for differing opinion; if he agrees, praise Allah.

The one seeking counsel's right is sincere advice with mercy and kindness. The counselor's right is gentleness and attentive listening. If right, praise Allah; if not, show compassion, do not accuse, know he erred, do not hold it against him unless deserving. There is no strength save in Allah. The elder's right is reverence for his age, honour for his precedence in Islam. Do not confront him in dispute or precede him. If he acts foolishly, bear it and honour him by Islam's right. The younger's right is compassion, teaching, pardoning, covering faults, kindness, and helping.

The asker's right is giving according to need. The one asked: if he gives, accept with gratitude; if withholds, accept his excuse. The one through whom Allah brings joy: first praise Allah, then thank him. The one who wrongs you: pardon him. If you know pardoning harms him, defend yourself. Allah says: 'And whoever defends himself after being wronged, upon those there is no way.'

The right of your creed's people is harbouring safety, compassion, kindness to their evildoers, drawing them close, reform, thanking their good-doers, keeping harm away. Love for them what you love for yourself. Their elders are like your father, youths like brothers, old women like your mother, children like your own. The right of the protected people is accepting from them what Allah accepted, and not wronging them while they fulfil Allah's covenant. There is no strength save in Allah.

key_terms.حق: Right, due, obligation — the central concept organizing this entire treatise
key_terms.رعية: Subjects, flock — those under one's care and authority
key_terms.طاعة الله: Obedience to God — the foundational principle underlying all other rights
key_terms.فتنة: Trial, test — used regarding the ruler's authority as a test from God

ai.seo_question: What is the Treatise on Rights (Risalat al-Huquq) by Imam Zayn al-Abidin?
ai.summary: This is the famous 'Treatise on Rights' (Risalat al-Huquq) by Imam Zayn al-Abidin (AS), the fourth Imam of the Shia. It is one of the most comprehensive ethical documents in Islamic literature, enumerating over fifty rights that a Muslim owes to God, to oneself, to one's body parts, to acts of worship, to family members, and to all members of society. Narrated through Abu Hamza al-Thumali, this treatise was addressed to the Imam's students and the broader Muslim community in Medina during the late first century AH.
